subject: Calling external script from within nimble model?

messages.author: c30f454051765351
messages.subject: Calling external script from within nimble model?
parts:
Hello All, 

I have a somewhat tricky project I am working on that links an integrated population model and integral projection model (ala Plard et al 2019). First, some background and then the tricky integration I could use some guidance on. 

Model 1 (IPMpop) is a Bayesian state-space integrated population model. The population I am working on has some demographic data such as estimated population counts, sex ratios, and survival. This model is coded in nimble and uses observed data from the population over the last 25-30 years. 

Model 2 (IPMind) is a bio-energetic integral projection model that links individual trait (body  mass and reserve mass) to demographic traits and population size. I am most interested in evaluating the impact of parasites and disease on demographics as mediated by their impact on body condition, so this IPMind is vital. This model is composed of survival, reproduction, growth, and development functions that estimate demographics based on the distribution of body size within the population. The problem is I dont have data for individual body size over time, so this model is based on a simulated initial population, I developed this based on the code of Lachish et al 2020. In its current form, there are a few scripts that are called from a final "run simulations" script to generate model output. 

Model 3 is what I am trying to figure out. Essentially, I want to improve the estimates of population size (n females) produced by the IPMind by modeling them as a function of the data in the Bayesian IPMpop. In theory, I could incorporate the IPMind into the Bayesian population model such that the projection kernel estimates population at each time step. For example, in the code below, M is the projection kernel that is estimated by the four R functions packaged into a single 'bigmatrix' function, zr and zs values are the trait value distributions (ie mesh points in an IPMind) and params are the IPM function parameters. So, population size at time t+1 would be a function of growth, survival and reproduction in time t. 

for(i in 1:nYears){
M <-  bigmatrix(zr_values, zs_values, params)
indPopVector[i+1]  <- M$G%*%(M$S*indPopVector[i]) + M$D%*%(M$R*indPopVector[i]) 
}

So, if that is built into the Bayesian IPMpop model in nimble, I should be able to model that as a function of the observed data with something like this, where ndat is the observed count data. 
for(i in 1:nndat){
    ndat[i,2] ~ T(dnorm(indPopVector[i], ndat[i,4]),0,550000) # Truncated normal
  }

In the simplest sense my question is whether it is possible to call external R functions from within a nimble model, or whether all of these would have to be recoded as nimbleFunctions? I have also been looking at the nimbleExternalcall and nimbleRcall functions, but given the complexity of what I have (multiple functions calling multiple scripts that set starting values etc) I am not sure how I'd make that work. 

If you've managed to read through to here, thanks! In my mind this seems like it should work, but as I stare into R and try to work out the mechanics of it all I get a bit overwhelmed. Any advice or thoughts will be much appreciated. I am happy to share some code off list if someone really wants to get into the weeds of it with me. 

Thanks, 
Ben

messages.subject: Re: Calling external script from within nimble model?
parts:
Hi Ben,

I don't think I have fully absorbed what you are trying to do, but I'm going to give a hasty answer in case it gives you enough.

First, a nimbleRcall really just creates a special wrapper or interface function between nimble and an R function.  That special function is a nimbleFunction, but you don't need to care about that.  The nimbleRcall mechanism is quite general except that inputs and outputs have to be numeric objects.

What I'm thinking might be helpful is to realize that you are free from within the nimbleRcall to manipulate the compiled model, or even the compiled samplers, as you wish.  The scheme in very quick outline would be like this:

myRfun <- function(x) { # From the nimbleRcall below, nimble will pack up the arguments for this function and take the return value. Otherwise it just calls your R function.
  # within this function, go ahead and manipulate cm if you want. e.g.
  cm$z <- x+1 # now this function sticks a wrench in the model by changing the values of x.  better know what you're doing statistically, but the code should work.
  # etc.
}

my_nimbleRcall <- nimbleRcall (myRfun.... etc)

m <- nimbleModel(...)
cm <- compileNimble(m). # This is what is used within myRfun

If you want to reach inside a sampler and, say, change a member variable, I could show you how to do that too.  But an alternative would be to put a nimbleRcall in the sampler and have it potentially get whatever information it needs from the R environment that way.

Again, I'm not quite sure of the complexity you need to solve.  Multiple functions calling multiple scripts doesn't sound like a problem.  You referred to setting starting values -- for what?

HTH.  If not, can you maybe say more about the code mechanics you want (regardless of the modeling intent)?

Perry

Hi Perry,

 

Thanks a lot for taking a stab at it despite my somewhat unclear questions. After thinking through things a bit more, I realize that there is really just one function I want to call within the nimblecode. I’ve also just finally just come to recognize why the nimble functions, or nimbleRcall are necessary – the R code needs to be compiled into the C language in order to work with the MCMC sampler. Sorry I’m a bit slow on that, I often forget all of the work arounds that are required to get an MCMC sampler working within R.

 

The one thing I’d like to incorporate into my nimble model is the `bigmatrix` function (code below), everything else just needs to be loaded in to the R environment prior to analysis. This bigmatrix function is a wrapper for the four demographic functions that define the population projections, so these functions would all need to be either written as nimbleFunctions, or translated to a nimbleFunction via nimbleRcall, as would the bigmatrix function itself.

 

I must admit I am not entirely up to speed on all the clever ways nimble models can be worked with and adapted. While I’ve used nimble for several projects I’ve always simply called the model code through nimbleMCMC rather than through the more adaptable multi-step process. That said, I want the inputs and outputs of this function to interact with different nodes of the model I already have, so I don’t know if it would be possible to call the model from within the nimbleRcall. Though, my understanding of all the details there is admittedly limited.

 

Thanks,

Ben

 

#################################################################

# FUNCTION TO CONSTRUCT COMPONENTS OF THE IPM KERNAL

################################################################

 

bigmatrix<-function(zr.values,zs.values, bigmatrix.params) {

  S <- Surv.fun(zr.values,zs.values, bigmatrix.params["surv_int"],

                  bigmatrix.params["surv_slope"], bigmatrix.params["starvation_ratio"],

                  bigmatrix.params["mean_ostertag"],bigmatrix.params["alfa_surv"],bigmatrix.params["theta_ost"])

 

  R <- Repro.fun(zr.values,zs.values, bigmatrix.params["zs_threshold_k"], bigmatrix.params["cmax_slope"],

                  bigmatrix.params["veg_energy"],bigmatrix.params["half_sat_val"],

                   bigmatrix.params["steepness"], bigmatrix.params["fat_threshold"],bigmatrix.params["burn_slope"],

                   bigmatrix.params["burn_add_summer"], bigmatrix.params["burn_add_winter"], bigmatrix.params["m_anabolism"],bigmatrix.params["m_catabolism"],

                   bigmatrix.params["breeding_zr_threshold"], bigmatrix.params["neonate_mortality"], params["Veg_max"], params["mean_warbles"],

                   bigmatrix.params["mean_ostertag"],bigmatrix.params["alfa_fecund"],bigmatrix.params["alfa_forage"], bigmatrix.params["insect_harass"],bigmatrix.params["theta_ost"])

 

  G <- G.fun(zr_50, zs_50,bigmatrix.params["cmax_slope"],bigmatrix.params["half_sat_val"],bigmatrix.params["steepness"],bigmatrix.params["fat_threshold"],bigmatrix.params["veg_energy"],

             bigmatrix.params["burn_slope"], bigmatrix.params["burn_add_summer"], bigmatrix.params["burn_add_winter"],bigmatrix.params["m_anabolism"], bigmatrix.params["m_catabolism"],

             bigmatrix.params["zs_threshold_k"], bigmatrix.params["breeding_zr_threshold"],bigmatrix.params["ZR_to_ReproZ"], bigmatrix.params["ZR_to_ZS"], bigmatrix.params["convert_coef_1"],

             bigmatrix.params["Veg_max"],bigmatrix.params["mean_warbles"],bigmatrix.params["mean_ostertag"],bigmatrix.params["alfa_forage"],bigmatrix.params["insect_harass"],bigmatrix.params["theta_ost"])

   

  D <- D.fun (zr_50, zs_50, bigmatrix.params["cmax_slope"],  bigmatrix.params["half_sat_val"], bigmatrix.params["steepness"],bigmatrix.params["fat_threshold"],

              bigmatrix.params["veg_energy"],bigmatrix.params["burn_slope"],bigmatrix.params["burn_add_summer"],bigmatrix.params["burn_add_winter"],

              bigmatrix.params["m_anabolism"], bigmatrix.params["m_catabolism"], bigmatrix.params["ReproZ_to_OffspringZS"], bigmatrix.params["convert_coef_2"],

              bigmatrix.params["ZR_to_ReproZ"], bigmatrix.params["convert_coef_3"], bigmatrix.params["Veg_max"],

              bigmatrix.params["mean_warbles"],bigmatrix.params["mean_ostertag"],bigmatrix.params["alfa_forage"], bigmatrix.params["insect_harass"],bigmatrix.params["theta_ost"])

 

  return(list(S=S,R=R,G=G,D=D))

}

Hi Ben,

 

I don't think I have fully absorbed what you are trying to do, but I'm going to give a hasty answer in case it gives you enough.

 

First, a nimbleRcall really just creates a special wrapper or interface function between nimble and an R function.  That special function is a nimbleFunction, but you don't need to care about that.  The nimbleRcall mechanism is quite general except that inputs and outputs have to be numeric objects.

 

What I'm thinking might be helpful is to realize that you are free from within the nimbleRcall to manipulate the compiled model, or even the compiled samplers, as you wish.  The scheme in very quick outline would be like this:

 

myRfun <- function(x) { # From the nimbleRcall below, nimble will pack up the arguments for this function and take the return value. Otherwise it just calls your R function.

  # within this function, go ahead and manipulate cm if you want. e.g.

  cm$z <- x+1 # now this function sticks a wrench in the model by changing the values of x.  better know what you're doing statistically, but the code should work.

  # etc.

}

 

my_nimbleRcall <- nimbleRcall (myRfun.... etc)

 

m <- nimbleModel(...)

cm <- compileNimble(m). # This is what is used within myRfun

 

If you want to reach inside a sampler and, say, change a member variable, I could show you how to do that too.  But an alternative would be to put a nimbleRcall in the sampler and have it potentially get whatever information it needs from the R environment that way.

 

Again, I'm not quite sure of the complexity you need to solve.  Multiple functions calling multiple scripts doesn't sound like a problem.  You referred to setting starting values -- for what?

 

HTH.  If not, can you maybe say more about the code mechanics you want (regardless of the modeling intent)?

 

Perry

Thanks, 

Ben

Hi Ben,

 

I was just looking at your previous message to reply and in popped your newest message just now.

 

For a nimbleFunction calling a nimbleFunction, there is a way to return a list and it is called (hah, surprise) a nimbleList.  I think it is relatively little used among nimbleFunction programmers, but it does exist and is important internally and is documented in the User Manual, so let me point you there to start.

nimbleCode({

...

S[1:N] <- Surv_fun_nimbleRcall_version(zr.values[1:A] , zs.values[1:B])

...

})

 

where I don't know the sizes or shapes of your model variables.

 

If there is redundant calculation in the steps needed, you could perhaps use memoize and/or caching methods to check inputs and make use of already calculated results from others of your functions.

Hi Ben,

 

I don't think I have fully absorbed what you are trying to do, but I'm going to give a hasty answer in case it gives you enough.

 

First, a nimbleRcall really just creates a special wrapper or interface function between nimble and an R function.  That special function is a nimbleFunction, but you don't need to care about that.  The nimbleRcall mechanism is quite general except that inputs and outputs have to be numeric objects.

 

What I'm thinking might be helpful is to realize that you are free from within the nimbleRcall to manipulate the compiled model, or even the compiled samplers, as you wish.  The scheme in very quick outline would be like this:

 

myRfun <- function(x) { # From the nimbleRcall below, nimble will pack up the arguments for this function and take the return value. Otherwise it just calls your R function.

  # within this function, go ahead and manipulate cm if you want. e.g.

  cm$z <- x+1 # now this function sticks a wrench in the model by changing the values of x.  better know what you're doing statistically, but the code should work.

  # etc.

}

 

my_nimbleRcall <- nimbleRcall (myRfun.... etc)

 

m <- nimbleModel(...)

cm <- compileNimble(m). # This is what is used within myRfun

 

If you want to reach inside a sampler and, say, change a member variable, I could show you how to do that too.  But an alternative would be to put a nimbleRcall in the sampler and have it potentially get whatever information it needs from the R environment that way.

 

Again, I'm not quite sure of the complexity you need to solve.  Multiple functions calling multiple scripts doesn't sound like a problem.  You referred to setting starting values -- for what?

 

HTH.  If not, can you maybe say more about the code mechanics you want (regardless of the modeling intent)?

 

Perry

Hello All, 

 

I have a somewhat tricky project I am working on that links an integrated population model and integral projection model (ala Plard et al 2019). First, some background and then the tricky integration I could use some guidance on. 

 

Model 1 (IPMpop) is a Bayesian state-space integrated population model. The population I am working on has some demographic data such as estimated population counts, sex ratios, and survival. This model is coded in nimble and uses observed data from the population over the last 25-30 years. 

 

Model 2 (IPMind) is a bio-energetic integral projection model that links individual trait (body  mass and reserve mass) to demographic traits and population size. I am most interested in evaluating the impact of parasites and disease on demographics as mediated by their impact on body condition, so this IPMind is vital. This model is composed of survival, reproduction, growth, and development functions that estimate demographics based on the distribution of body size within the population. The problem is I dont have data for individual body size over time, so this model is based on a simulated initial population, I developed this based on the code of Lachish et al 2020. In its current form, there are a few scripts that are called from a final "run simulations" script to generate model output. 

 

Model 3 is what I am trying to figure out. Essentially, I want to improve the estimates of population size (n females) produced by the IPMind by modeling them as a function of the data in the Bayesian IPMpop. In theory, I could incorporate the IPMind into the Bayesian population model such that the projection kernel estimates population at each time step. For example, in the code below, M is the projection kernel that is estimated by the four R functions packaged into a single 'bigmatrix' function, zr and zs values are the trait value distributions (ie mesh points in an IPMind) and params are the IPM function parameters. So, population size at time t+1 would be a function of growth, survival and reproduction in time t. 

 

for(i in 1:nYears){

M <-  bigmatrix(zr_values, zs_values, params)

indPopVector[i+1]  <- M$G%*%(M$S*indPopVector[i]) + M$D%*%(M$R*indPopVector[i]) 

}

 

So, if that is built into the Bayesian IPMpop model in nimble, I should be able to model that as a function of the observed data with something like this, where ndat is the observed count data. 

for(i in 1:nndat){
    ndat[i,2] ~ T(dnorm(indPopVector[i], ndat[i,4]),0,550000) # Truncated normal
  }

 

In the simplest sense my question is whether it is possible to call external R functions from within a nimble model, or whether all of these would have to be recoded as nimbleFunctions? I have also been looking at the nimbleExternalcall and nimbleRcall functions, but given the complexity of what I have (multiple functions calling multiple scripts that set starting values etc) I am not sure how I'd make that work. 

 

If you've managed to read through to here, thanks! In my mind this seems like it should work, but as I stare into R and try to work out the mechanics of it all I get a bit overwhelmed. Any advice or thoughts will be much appreciated. I am happy to share some code off list if someone really wants to get into the weeds of it with me. 

 

Thanks, 

Ben

Model 1 (IPMpop) is a Bayesian state-space integrated population model. The population I am working on has some demographic data such as estimated population counts, sex ratios, and survival. This model is coded in nimble and uses observed data from the population over the last 25-30 years. 

 

Model 2 (IPMind) is a bio-energetic integral projection model that links individual trait (body  mass and reserve mass) to demographic traits and population size. I am most interested in evaluating the impact of parasites and disease on demographics as mediated by their impact on body condition, so this IPMind is vital. This model is composed of survival, reproduction, growth, and development functions that estimate demographics based on the distribution of body size within the population. The problem is I dont have data for individual body size over time, so this model is based on a simulated initial population, I developed this based on the code of Lachish et al 2020. In its current form, there are a few scripts that are called from a final "run simulations" script to generate model output. 

 

Model 3 is what I am trying to figure out. Essentially, I want to improve the estimates of population size (n females) produced by the IPMind by modeling them as a function of the data in the Bayesian IPMpop. In theory, I could incorporate the IPMind into the Bayesian population model such that the projection kernel estimates population at each time step. For example, in the code below, M is the projection kernel that is estimated by the four R functions packaged into a single 'bigmatrix' function, zr and zs values are the trait value distributions (ie mesh points in an IPMind) and params are the IPM function parameters. So, population size at time t+1 would be a function of growth, survival and reproduction in time t. 

 

for(i in 1:nYears){

M <-  bigmatrix(zr_values, zs_values, params)

indPopVector[i+1]  <- M$G%*%(M$S*indPopVector[i]) + M$D%*%(M$R*indPopVector[i]) 

}

 

So, if that is built into the Bayesian IPMpop model in nimble, I should be able to model that as a function of the observed data with something like this, where ndat is the observed count data. 

for(i in 1:nndat){
    ndat[i,2] ~ T(dnorm(indPopVector[i], ndat[i,4]),0,550000) # Truncated normal
  }

 

In the simplest sense my question is whether it is possible to call external R functions from within a nimble model, or whether all of these would have to be recoded as nimbleFunctions? I have also been looking at the nimbleExternalcall and nimbleRcall functions, but given the complexity of what I have (multiple functions calling multiple scripts that set starting values etc) I am not sure how I'd make that work. 

 

If you've managed to read through to here, thanks! In my mind this seems like it should work, but as I stare into R and try to work out the mechanics of it all I get a bit overwhelmed. Any advice or thoughts will be much appreciated. I am happy to share some code off list if someone really wants to get into the weeds of it with me. 

 

Thanks, 

Ben

Hi Ben,

 

I was just looking at your previous message to reply and in popped your newest message just now.

 

For a nimbleFunction calling a nimbleFunction, there is a way to return a list and it is called (hah, surprise) a nimbleList.  I think it is relatively little used among nimbleFunction programmers, but it does exist and is important internally and is documented in the User Manual, so let me point you there to start.

 

However, a node in a nimbleModel can't be a nimbleList.  It can only be a (non-scalar) numeric object.  So if you want to use your functions in a model, you would indeed need to break the pieces into different functions.  I think it would look like:

 

nimbleCode({

...

S[1:N] <- Surv_fun_nimbleRcall_version(zr.values[1:A] , zs.values[1:B])

...

})

 

where I don't know the sizes or shapes of your model variables.

 

If there is redundant calculation in the steps needed, you could perhaps use memoize and/or caching methods to check inputs and make use of already calculated results from others of your functions.

 

If you know all of your four pieces (S, R, G, D) only ever need to be calculated at the same time (i.e. they are in the same position in the model graph), some options are (1) you could stack them into one model variable and use indexing to make use of the pieces you need elsewhere, or (2) you could create dummy declarations for all but one of them ( to ensure they exist in the model ) and then make the single non-dummy one have its R function put new values into the others.  That is short-circuiting things but would work fine.  Let me know if that is too cryptic of an explanation.

 

I am not clear what bigmatrix.params is.  I think it is something you'd be accessing not from the model but rather from the R environment, right?

 

Perry

Hi Ben,

 

I don't think I have fully absorbed what you are trying to do, but I'm going to give a hasty answer in case it gives you enough.

 

First, a nimbleRcall really just creates a special wrapper or interface function between nimble and an R function.  That special function is a nimbleFunction, but you don't need to care about that.  The nimbleRcall mechanism is quite general except that inputs and outputs have to be numeric objects.

 

What I'm thinking might be helpful is to realize that you are free from within the nimbleRcall to manipulate the compiled model, or even the compiled samplers, as you wish.  The scheme in very quick outline would be like this:

 

myRfun <- function(x) { # From the nimbleRcall below, nimble will pack up the arguments for this function and take the return value. Otherwise it just calls your R function.

  # within this function, go ahead and manipulate cm if you want. e.g.

  cm$z <- x+1 # now this function sticks a wrench in the model by changing the values of x.  better know what you're doing statistically, but the code should work.

  # etc.

}

 

my_nimbleRcall <- nimbleRcall (myRfun.... etc)

 

m <- nimbleModel(...)

cm <- compileNimble(m). # This is what is used within myRfun

 

If you want to reach inside a sampler and, say, change a member variable, I could show you how to do that too.  But an alternative would be to put a nimbleRcall in the sampler and have it potentially get whatever information it needs from the R environment that way.

 

Again, I'm not quite sure of the complexity you need to solve.  Multiple functions calling multiple scripts doesn't sound like a problem.  You referred to setting starting values -- for what?

 

HTH.  If not, can you maybe say more about the code mechanics you want (regardless of the modeling intent)?

 

Perry

Hi Ben,

 

I don't think I have fully absorbed what you are trying to do, but I'm going to give a hasty answer in case it gives you enough.

 

First, a nimbleRcall really just creates a special wrapper or interface function between nimble and an R function.  That special function is a nimbleFunction, but you don't need to care about that.  The nimbleRcall mechanism is quite general except that inputs and outputs have to be numeric objects.

 

What I'm thinking might be helpful is to realize that you are free from within the nimbleRcall to manipulate the compiled model, or even the compiled samplers, as you wish.  The scheme in very quick outline would be like this:

 

myRfun <- function(x) { # From the nimbleRcall below, nimble will pack up the arguments for this function and take the return value. Otherwise it just calls your R function.

  # within this function, go ahead and manipulate cm if you want. e.g.

  cm$z <- x+1 # now this function sticks a wrench in the model by changing the values of x.  better know what you're doing statistically, but the code should work.

  # etc.

}

 

my_nimbleRcall <- nimbleRcall (myRfun.... etc)

 

m <- nimbleModel(...)

cm <- compileNimble(m). # This is what is used within myRfun

 

If you want to reach inside a sampler and, say, change a member variable, I could show you how to do that too.  But an alternative would be to put a nimbleRcall in the sampler and have it potentially get whatever information it needs from the R environment that way.

 

Again, I'm not quite sure of the complexity you need to solve.  Multiple functions calling multiple scripts doesn't sound like a problem.  You referred to setting starting values -- for what?

 

HTH.  If not, can you maybe say more about the code mechanics you want (regardless of the modeling intent)?

 

Perry

Hi Ben,

 

I was just looking at your previous message to reply and in popped your newest message just now.

 

For a nimbleFunction calling a nimbleFunction, there is a way to return a list and it is called (hah, surprise) a nimbleList.  I think it is relatively little used among nimbleFunction programmers, but it does exist and is important internally and is documented in the User Manual, so let me point you there to start.

 

However, a node in a nimbleModel can't be a nimbleList.  It can only be a (non-scalar) numeric object.  So if you want to use your functions in a model, you would indeed need to break the pieces into different functions.  I think it would look like:

 

nimbleCode({

...

S[1:N] <- Surv_fun_nimbleRcall_version(zr.values[1:A] , zs.values[1:B])

...

})

 

where I don't know the sizes or shapes of your model variables.

 

If there is redundant calculation in the steps needed, you could perhaps use memoize and/or caching methods to check inputs and make use of already calculated results from others of your functions.

 

If you know all of your four pieces (S, R, G, D) only ever need to be calculated at the same time (i.e. they are in the same position in the model graph), some options are (1) you could stack them into one model variable and use indexing to make use of the pieces you need elsewhere, or (2) you could create dummy declarations for all but one of them ( to ensure they exist in the model ) and then make the single non-dummy one have its R function put new values into the others.  That is short-circuiting things but would work fine.  Let me know if that is too cryptic of an explanation.

 

I am not clear what bigmatrix.params is.  I think it is something you'd be accessing not from the model but rather from the R environment, right?

 

Perry

 This was part of the call:  eigenBlock(ARG1_S_,1:2500) * pVec[1:2500]

This error catch tells me pVec has the wrong number of dimensions.
I see pVec is created from
pVec <- G[1:2500,1:2500] %*% (S[1:2500]*popVec)
which will return a matrix.  (This is true in R as well, but R can dynamically treat that later as a vector whereas nimbleFunctions must have statically [unchanging] types.)
There is a section in the user manual on dimension mismatches that can trip people up and how to handle them.  In your case, one solution would be:

pVec <- G[1:2500,1:2500] %*% (S[1:2500]*popVec)[,1]

where the "[,1]" has the effect of dropping a dimension and returning a vector.  You could then do the same in the next line.

You do also need a returnType statement.

The requirement to always explicitly index non-scalar objects is only for model code.  nimbleFunctions do not need that.

I also noticed you need to access seas2sim[1] to use it as a scalar.

Here is a modification that works:

getPopVec <- nimbleFunction(run = function(S = double(1),R = double(1),G = double(2),D = double(2), popVec = double(1),seas2sim = double(1)){
    returnType(double(1))
    pVec <- (G %*% (S*popVec))[,1]
    if(seas2sim[1] == 2) pVec <- (G %*% (S*pVec))[,1] + (D %*% (R*pVec))[,1]
    return(pVec)
})
CgetPopVec <- compileNimble(getPopVec)

Does that look like what you need?
Perry

I was just looking at your previous message to reply and in popped your newest message just now.

 

For a nimbleFunction calling a nimbleFunction, there is a way to return a list and it is called (hah, surprise) a nimbleList.  I think it is relatively little used among nimbleFunction programmers, but it does exist and is important internally and is documented in the User Manual, so let me point you there to start.

 

However, a node in a nimbleModel can't be a nimbleList.  It can only be a (non-scalar) numeric object.  So if you want to use your functions in a model, you would indeed need to break the pieces into different functions.  I think it would look like:

 

nimbleCode({

...

S[1:N] <- Surv_fun_nimbleRcall_version(zr.values[1:A] , zs.values[1:B])

...

})

 

where I don't know the sizes or shapes of your model variables.

 

If there is redundant calculation in the steps needed, you could perhaps use memoize and/or caching methods to check inputs and make use of already calculated results from others of your functions.

 

If you know all of your four pieces (S, R, G, D) only ever need to be calculated at the same time (i.e. they are in the same position in the model graph), some options are (1) you could stack them into one model variable and use indexing to make use of the pieces you need elsewhere, or (2) you could create dummy declarations for all but one of them ( to ensure they exist in the model ) and then make the single non-dummy one have its R function put new values into the others.  That is short-circuiting things but would work fine.  Let me know if that is too cryptic of an explanation.

 

I am not clear what bigmatrix.params is.  I think it is something you'd be accessing not from the model but rather from the R environment, right?

 

Perry

Hi Ben,

 

I don't think I have fully absorbed what you are trying to do, but I'm going to give a hasty answer in case it gives you enough.

 

First, a nimbleRcall really just creates a special wrapper or interface function between nimble and an R function.  That special function is a nimbleFunction, but you don't need to care about that.  The nimbleRcall mechanism is quite general except that inputs and outputs have to be numeric objects.

 

What I'm thinking might be helpful is to realize that you are free from within the nimbleRcall to manipulate the compiled model, or even the compiled samplers, as you wish.  The scheme in very quick outline would be like this:

 

myRfun <- function(x) { # From the nimbleRcall below, nimble will pack up the arguments for this function and take the return value. Otherwise it just calls your R function.

  # within this function, go ahead and manipulate cm if you want. e.g.

  cm$z <- x+1 # now this function sticks a wrench in the model by changing the values of x.  better know what you're doing statistically, but the code should work.

  # etc.

}

 

my_nimbleRcall <- nimbleRcall (myRfun.... etc)

 

m <- nimbleModel(...)

cm <- compileNimble(m). # This is what is used within myRfun

 

If you want to reach inside a sampler and, say, change a member variable, I could show you how to do that too.  But an alternative would be to put a nimbleRcall in the sampler and have it potentially get whatever information it needs from the R environment that way.

 

Again, I'm not quite sure of the complexity you need to solve.  Multiple functions calling multiple scripts doesn't sound like a problem.  You referred to setting starting values -- for what?

 

HTH.  If not, can you maybe say more about the code mechanics you want (regardless of the modeling intent)?

 

Perry

There is a section in the user manual on dimension mismatches that can trip people up and how to handle them.  In your case, one solution would be:

 

pVec <- G[1:2500,1:2500] %*% (S[1:2500]*popVec)[,1]

 

where the "[,1]" has the effect of dropping a dimension and returning a vector.  You could then do the same in the next line.

 

You do also need a returnType statement.

 

The requirement to always explicitly index non-scalar objects is only for model code.  nimbleFunctions do not need that.

 

I also noticed you need to access seas2sim[1] to use it as a scalar.

 

Here is a modification that works:

 

getPopVec <- nimbleFunction(run = function(S = double(1),R = double(1),G = double(2),D = double(2), popVec = double(1),seas2sim = double(1)){
    returnType(double(1))
    pVec <- (G %*% (S*popVec))[,1]
    if(seas2sim[1] == 2) pVec <- (G %*% (S*pVec))[,1] + (D %*% (R*pVec))[,1]
    return(pVec)
})

CgetPopVec <- compileNimble(getPopVec)

 

Does that look like what you need?

Perry

For a nimbleFunction calling a nimbleFunction, there is a way to return a list and it is called (hah, surprise) a nimbleList.  I think it is relatively little used among nimbleFunction programmers, but it does exist and is important internally and is documented in the User Manual, so let me point you there to start.

 

However, a node in a nimbleModel can't be a nimbleList.  It can only be a (non-scalar) numeric object.  So if you want to use your functions in a model, you would indeed need to break the pieces into different functions.  I think it would look like:

 

nimbleCode({

...

S[1:N] <- Surv_fun_nimbleRcall_version(zr.values[1:A] , zs.values[1:B])

...

})

 

where I don't know the sizes or shapes of your model variables.

 

If there is redundant calculation in the steps needed, you could perhaps use memoize and/or caching methods to check inputs and make use of already calculated results from others of your functions.

 

If you know all of your four pieces (S, R, G, D) only ever need to be calculated at the same time (i.e. they are in the same position in the model graph), some options are (1) you could stack them into one model variable and use indexing to make use of the pieces you need elsewhere, or (2) you could create dummy declarations for all but one of them ( to ensure they exist in the model ) and then make the single non-dummy one have its R function put new values into the others.  That is short-circuiting things but would work fine.  Let me know if that is too cryptic of an explanation.

 

I am not clear what bigmatrix.params is.  I think it is something you'd be accessing not from the model but rather from the R environment, right?

Hi Ben,

 

I don't think I have fully absorbed what you are trying to do, but I'm going to give a hasty answer in case it gives you enough.

 

First, a nimbleRcall really just creates a special wrapper or interface function between nimble and an R function.  That special function is a nimbleFunction, but you don't need to care about that.  The nimbleRcall mechanism is quite general except that inputs and outputs have to be numeric objects.

 

What I'm thinking might be helpful is to realize that you are free from within the nimbleRcall to manipulate the compiled model, or even the compiled samplers, as you wish.  The scheme in very quick outline would be like this:

 

myRfun <- function(x) { # From the nimbleRcall below, nimble will pack up the arguments for this function and take the return value. Otherwise it just calls your R function.

  # within this function, go ahead and manipulate cm if you want. e.g.

  cm$z <- x+1 # now this function sticks a wrench in the model by changing the values of x.  better know what you're doing statistically, but the code should work.

  # etc.

}

 

my_nimbleRcall <- nimbleRcall (myRfun.... etc)

 

m <- nimbleModel(...)

cm <- compileNimble(m). # This is what is used within myRfun

 

If you want to reach inside a sampler and, say, change a member variable, I could show you how to do that too.  But an alternative would be to put a nimbleRcall in the sampler and have it potentially get whatever information it needs from the R environment that way.

 

Again, I'm not quite sure of the complexity you need to solve.  Multiple functions calling multiple scripts doesn't sound like a problem.  You referred to setting starting values -- for what?

 

HTH.  If not, can you maybe say more about the code mechanics you want (regardless of the modeling intent)?

 

Perry

I am most interested in evaluating the impact of parasites and disease on demographics as mediated by their impact on body condition, so this IPMind is vital. This model is composed of survival, reproduction, growth, and development functions that estimate demographics based on the distribution of body size within the population. The problem is I dont have data for individual body size over time, so this model is based on a simulated initial population, I developed this based on the code of Lachish et al 2020. In its current form, there are a few scripts that are called from a final "run simulations" script to generate model output. 

 

Model 3 is what I am trying to figure out. Essentially, I want to improve the estimates of population size (n females) produced by the IPMind by modeling them as a function of the data in the Bayesian IPMpop. In theory, I could incorporate the IPMind into the Bayesian population model such that the projection kernel estimates population at each time step. For example, in the code below, M is the projection kernel that is estimated by the four R functions packaged into a single 'bigmatrix' function, zr and zs values are the trait value distributions (ie mesh points in an IPMind) and params are the IPM function parameters. M <-  bigmatrix(zr_values, zs_values, params)

indPopVector[i+1]  <- M$G%*%(M$S*indPopVector[i]) + M$D%*%(M$R*indPopVector[i])

In the simplest sense my question is whether it is possible to call external R functions from within a nimble model, or whether all of these would have to be recoded as nimbleFunctions? I have also been looking at the nimbleExternalcall and nimbleRcall functions, but given the complexity of what I have (multiple functions calling multiple scripts that set starting values etc) I am not sure how I'd make that work. 

 

If you've managed to read through to here, thanks! In my mind this seems like it should work, but as I stare into R and try to work out the mechanics of it all I get a bit overwhelmed. Any advice or thoughts will be much appreciated. I am happy to share some code off list if someone really wants to get into the weeds of it with me. 

 

Thanks, 

Ben

Here's my process.  

 

CgetPopVec <- compileNimble(getPopVec)

 

Output is:

Compiling
  [Note] This may take a minute.
  [Note] Use 'showCompilerOutput = TRUE' to see C++ compilation details.
Error: Error, wrong number of indices provided for pVec[1:2500].
 This occurred for: pVec[1:2500]
 This was part of the call:  eigenBlock(ARG1_S_,1:2500) * pVec[1:2500]

 

This error catch tells me pVec has the wrong number of dimensions.

I see pVec is created from

pVec <- G[1:2500,1:2500] %*% (S[1:2500]*popVec)

which will return a matrix.  (This is true in R as well, but R can dynamically treat that later as a vector whereas nimbleFunctions must have statically [unchanging] types.)

There is a section in the user manual on dimension mismatches that can trip people up and how to handle them.  In your case, one solution would be:

 

pVec <- G[1:2500,1:2500] %*% (S[1:2500]*popVec)[,1]

 

where the "[,1]" has the effect of dropping a dimension and returning a vector.  You could then do the same in the next line.

 

You do also need a returnType statement.

 

The requirement to always explicitly index non-scalar objects is only for model code.  nimbleFunctions do not need that.

 

I also noticed you need to access seas2sim[1] to use it as a scalar.

 

Here is a modification that works:

 

getPopVec <- nimbleFunction(run = function(S = double(1),R = double(1),G = double(2),D = double(2), popVec = double(1),seas2sim = double(1)){
    returnType(double(1))
    pVec <- (G %*% (S*popVec))[,1]
    if(seas2sim[1] == 2) pVec <- (G %*% (S*pVec))[,1] + (D %*% (R*pVec))[,1]
    return(pVec)
})

CgetPopVec <- compileNimble(getPopVec)

 

Does that look like what you need?

Perry

I was just looking at your previous message to reply and in popped your newest message just now.

 

For a nimbleFunction calling a nimbleFunction, there is a way to return a list and it is called (hah, surprise) a nimbleList.  I think it is relatively little used among nimbleFunction programmers, but it does exist and is important internally and is documented in the User Manual, so let me point you there to start.

 

However, a node in a nimbleModel can't be a nimbleList.  It can only be a (non-scalar) numeric object.  So if you want to use your functions in a model, you would indeed need to break the pieces into different functions.  I think it would look like:

 

nimbleCode({

...

S[1:N] <- Surv_fun_nimbleRcall_version(zr.values[1:A] , zs.values[1:B])

...

})

 

where I don't know the sizes or shapes of your model variables.

 

If there is redundant calculation in the steps needed, you could perhaps use memoize and/or caching methods to check inputs and make use of already calculated results from others of your functions.

 

If you know all of your four pieces (S, R, G, D) only ever need to be calculated at the same time (i.e. they are in the same position in the model graph), some options are (1) you could stack them into one model variable and use indexing to make use of the pieces you need elsewhere, or (2) you could create dummy declarations for all but one of them ( to ensure they exist in the model ) and then make the single non-dummy one have its R function put new values into the others.  That is short-circuiting things but would work fine.  Let me know if that is too cryptic of an explanation.

 

I am not clear what bigmatrix.params is.  I think it is something you'd be accessing not from the model but rather from the R environment, right?

 

Perry

Hi Ben,

 

I don't think I have fully absorbed what you are trying to do, but I'm going to give a hasty answer in case it gives you enough.

 

First, a nimbleRcall really just creates a special wrapper or interface function between nimble and an R function.  That special function is a nimbleFunction, but you don't need to care about that.  The nimbleRcall mechanism is quite general except that inputs and outputs have to be numeric objects.

 

What I'm thinking might be helpful is to realize that you are free from within the nimbleRcall to manipulate the compiled model, or even the compiled samplers, as you wish.  The scheme in very quick outline would be like this:

 

myRfun <- function(x) { # From the nimbleRcall below, nimble will pack up the arguments for this function and take the return value. Otherwise it just calls your R function.

  # within this function, go ahead and manipulate cm if you want. e.g.

  cm$z <- x+1 # now this function sticks a wrench in the model by changing the values of x.  better know what you're doing statistically, but the code should work.

  # etc.

}

 

my_nimbleRcall <- nimbleRcall (myRfun.... etc)

 

m <- nimbleModel(...)

cm <- compileNimble(m). # This is what is used within myRfun

 

If you want to reach inside a sampler and, say, change a member variable, I could show you how to do that too.  But an alternative would be to put a nimbleRcall in the sampler and have it potentially get whatever information it needs from the R environment that way.

 

Again, I'm not quite sure of the complexity you need to solve.  Multiple functions calling multiple scripts doesn't sound like a problem.  You referred to setting starting values -- for what?

 

HTH.  If not, can you maybe say more about the code mechanics you want (regardless of the modeling intent)?

 

Perry

Hi Ben,

We try to have errors trapped in R before they result in a C++ compilation failure, but clearly that wasn't successful here.

I think it is telling you that "2" is not a vector.  You could change the type declaration for that argument to double(0) or integer(0) (and then use it simply as a vector), or you could put c(2) to turn it into a vector of length 1.  Confusion between true scalars (which don't really exist in R) and length-1 vectors is a point of friction.

A good way to test and debug outside of a model is to write a second nimbleFunction to call getPopVec and try compiling them together.  Then you can confirm that how you call it works.  Another debugging route is to make the behavior incomplete and build up bits at a time.  E.g. start with a function that takes one argument and does something trivial and build up from there.  But I'm not saying that we're happy with seeing this slip through error-trapping and give you a C++ error.  It's something we should catch better.

HTH
Perry

Here's my process.

Output is:

Compiling

Error: Error, wrong number of indices provided for pVec[1:2500].
 This occurred for: pVec[1:2500]
 This was part of the call:  eigenBlock(ARG1_S_,1:2500) * pVec[1:2500]

 

This error catch tells me pVec has the wrong number of dimensions.

I see pVec is created from

pVec <- G[1:2500,1:2500] %*% (S[1:2500]*popVec)

which will return a matrix.  (This is true in R as well, but R can dynamically treat that later as a vector whereas nimbleFunctions must have statically [unchanging] types.)

There is a section in the user manual on dimension mismatches that can trip people up and how to handle them.  In your case, one solution would be:

 

pVec <- G[1:2500,1:2500] %*% (S[1:2500]*popVec)[,1]

 

where the "[,1]" has the effect of dropping a dimension and returning a vector.  You could then do the same in the next line.

 

You do also need a returnType statement.

 

The requirement to always explicitly index non-scalar objects is only for model code.  nimbleFunctions do not need that.

 

I also noticed you need to access seas2sim[1] to use it as a scalar.

 

Here is a modification that works:

 

getPopVec <- nimbleFunction(run = function(S = double(1),R = double(1),G = double(2),D = double(2), popVec = double(1),seas2sim = double(1)){
    returnType(double(1))
    pVec <- (G %*% (S*popVec))[,1]
    if(seas2sim[1] == 2) pVec <- (G %*% (S*pVec))[,1] + (D %*% (R*pVec))[,1]
    return(pVec)
})

CgetPopVec <- compileNimble(getPopVec)

 

Does that look like what you need?

Perry

For a nimbleFunction calling a nimbleFunction, there is a way to return a list and it is called (hah, surprise) a nimbleList.  I think it is relatively little used among nimbleFunction programmers, but it does exist and is important internally and is documented in the User Manual, so let me point you there to start.

nimbleCode({

...

S[1:N] <- Surv_fun_nimbleRcall_version(zr.values[1:A] , zs.values[1:B])

...

})

 

where I don't know the sizes or shapes of your model variables.

Hi Ben,

 

I don't think I have fully absorbed what you are trying to do, but I'm going to give a hasty answer in case it gives you enough.

 

First, a nimbleRcall really just creates a special wrapper or interface function between nimble and an R function.  That special function is a nimbleFunction, but you don't need to care about that.  The nimbleRcall mechanism is quite general except that inputs and outputs have to be numeric objects.

 

What I'm thinking might be helpful is to realize that you are free from within the nimbleRcall to manipulate the compiled model, or even the compiled samplers, as you wish.  The scheme in very quick outline would be like this:

 

myRfun <- function(x) { # From the nimbleRcall below, nimble will pack up the arguments for this function and take the return value. Otherwise it just calls your R function.

  # within this function, go ahead and manipulate cm if you want. e.g.

  cm$z <- x+1 # now this function sticks a wrench in the model by changing the values of x.  better know what you're doing statistically, but the code should work.

  # etc.

}

 

my_nimbleRcall <- nimbleRcall (myRfun.... etc)

 

m <- nimbleModel(...)

cm <- compileNimble(m). # This is what is used within myRfun

 

If you want to reach inside a sampler and, say, change a member variable, I could show you how to do that too.  But an alternative would be to put a nimbleRcall in the sampler and have it potentially get whatever information it needs from the R environment that way.

 

Again, I'm not quite sure of the complexity you need to solve.  Multiple functions calling multiple scripts doesn't sound like a problem.  You referred to setting starting values -- for what?

 

HTH.  If not, can you maybe say more about the code mechanics you want (regardless of the modeling intent)?

 

Perry

Hi Ben,

 

We try to have errors trapped in R before they result in a C++ compilation failure, but clearly that wasn't successful here.

 

I think it is telling you that "2" is not a vector.  You could change the type declaration for that argument to double(0) or integer(0) (and then use it simply as a vector), or you could put c(2) to turn it into a vector of length 1.  Confusion between true scalars (which don't really exist in R) and length-1 vectors is a point of friction.

 

A good way to test and debug outside of a model is to write a second nimbleFunction to call getPopVec and try compiling them together.  Then you can confirm that how you call it works.  Another debugging route is to make the behavior incomplete and build up bits at a time.  E.g. start with a function that takes one argument and does something trivial and build up from there.  But I'm not saying that we're happy with seeing this slip through error-trapping and give you a C++ error.  It's something we should catch better.

 

HTH

Perry

Here's my process.

Output is:

Compiling

Error: Error, wrong number of indices provided for pVec[1:2500].
 This occurred for: pVec[1:2500]
 This was part of the call:  eigenBlock(ARG1_S_,1:2500) * pVec[1:2500]

 

This error catch tells me pVec has the wrong number of dimensions.

I see pVec is created from

pVec <- G[1:2500,1:2500] %*% (S[1:2500]*popVec)

which will return a matrix.  (This is true in R as well, but R can dynamically treat that later as a vector whereas nimbleFunctions must have statically [unchanging] types.)

There is a section in the user manual on dimension mismatches that can trip people up and how to handle them.  In your case, one solution would be:

 

pVec <- G[1:2500,1:2500] %*% (S[1:2500]*popVec)[,1]

 

where the "[,1]" has the effect of dropping a dimension and returning a vector.  You could then do the same in the next line.

 

You do also need a returnType statement.

 

The requirement to always explicitly index non-scalar objects is only for model code.  nimbleFunctions do not need that.

 

I also noticed you need to access seas2sim[1] to use it as a scalar.

 

Here is a modification that works:

 

getPopVec <- nimbleFunction(run = function(S = double(1),R = double(1),G = double(2),D = double(2), popVec = double(1),seas2sim = double(1)){
    returnType(double(1))
    pVec <- (G %*% (S*popVec))[,1]
    if(seas2sim[1] == 2) pVec <- (G %*% (S*pVec))[,1] + (D %*% (R*pVec))[,1]
    return(pVec)
})

CgetPopVec <- compileNimble(getPopVec)

 

Does that look like what you need?

Perry

For a nimbleFunction calling a nimbleFunction, there is a way to return a list and it is called (hah, surprise) a nimbleList.  I think it is relatively little used among nimbleFunction programmers, but it does exist and is important internally and is documented in the User Manual, so let me point you there to start.

 

However, a node in a nimbleModel can't be a nimbleList.  It can only be a (non-scalar) numeric object.  So if you want to use your functions in a model, you would indeed need to break the pieces into different functions.  I think it would look like:

 

nimbleCode({

...

S[1:N] <- Surv_fun_nimbleRcall_version(zr.values[1:A] , zs.values[1:B])

...

})

 

where I don't know the sizes or shapes of your model variables.

 

If there is redundant calculation in the steps needed, you could perhaps use memoize and/or caching methods to check inputs and make use of already calculated results from others of your functions.

 

If you know all of your four pieces (S, R, G, D) only ever need to be calculated at the same time (i.e. they are in the same position in the model graph), some options are (1) you could stack them into one model variable and use indexing to make use of the pieces you need elsewhere, or (2) you could create dummy declarations for all but one of them ( to ensure they exist in the model ) and then make the single non-dummy one have its R function put new values into the others.  That is short-circuiting things but would work fine.  Let me know if that is too cryptic of an explanation.

Hi Ben,

 

I don't think I have fully absorbed what you are trying to do, but I'm going to give a hasty answer in case it gives you enough.

 

First, a nimbleRcall really just creates a special wrapper or interface function between nimble and an R function.  That special function is a nimbleFunction, but you don't need to care about that.  The nimbleRcall mechanism is quite general except that inputs and outputs have to be numeric objects.

 

What I'm thinking might be helpful is to realize that you are free from within the nimbleRcall to manipulate the compiled model, or even the compiled samplers, as you wish.  The scheme in very quick outline would be like this:

 

myRfun <- function(x) { # From the nimbleRcall below, nimble will pack up the arguments for this function and take the return value. Otherwise it just calls your R function.

  # within this function, go ahead and manipulate cm if you want. e.g.

  cm$z <- x+1 # now this function sticks a wrench in the model by changing the values of x.  better know what you're doing statistically, but the code should work.

  # etc.

}

 

my_nimbleRcall <- nimbleRcall (myRfun.... etc)

 

m <- nimbleModel(...)

cm <- compileNimble(m). # This is what is used within myRfun

 

If you want to reach inside a sampler and, say, change a member variable, I could show you how to do that too.  But an alternative would be to put a nimbleRcall in the sampler and have it potentially get whatever information it needs from the R environment that way.

 

Again, I'm not quite sure of the complexity you need to solve.  Multiple functions calling multiple scripts doesn't sound like a problem.  You referred to setting starting values -- for what?

 

HTH.  If not, can you maybe say more about the code mechanics you want (regardless of the modeling intent)?

 

Perry

We try to have errors trapped in R before they result in a C++ compilation failure, but clearly that wasn't successful here.

 

I think it is telling you that "2" is not a vector.  You could change the type declaration for that argument to double(0) or integer(0) (and then use it simply as a vector), or you could put c(2) to turn it into a vector of length 1.  Confusion between true scalars (which don't really exist in R) and length-1 vectors is a point of friction.

 

A good way to test and debug outside of a model is to write a second nimbleFunction to call getPopVec and try compiling them together.  Then you can confirm that how you call it works.  Another debugging route is to make the behavior incomplete and build up bits at a time.  E.g. start with a function that takes one argument and does something trivial and build up from there.  But I'm not saying that we're happy with seeing this slip through error-trapping and give you a C++ error.  It's something we should catch better.

 

HTH

Perry

Output is:

Compiling
  [Note] This may take a minute.
  [Note] Use 'showCompilerOutput = TRUE' to see C++ compilation details.
Error: Error, wrong number of indices provided for pVec[1:2500].
 This occurred for: pVec[1:2500]
 This was part of the call:  eigenBlock(ARG1_S_,1:2500) * pVec[1:2500]

 

This error catch tells me pVec has the wrong number of dimensions.

I see pVec is created from

pVec <- G[1:2500,1:2500] %*% (S[1:2500]*popVec)

which will return a matrix.  (This is true in R as well, but R can dynamically treat that later as a vector whereas nimbleFunctions must have statically [unchanging] types.)

There is a section in the user manual on dimension mismatches that can trip people up and how to handle them.  In your case, one solution would be:

 

pVec <- G[1:2500,1:2500] %*% (S[1:2500]*popVec)[,1]

 

where the "[,1]" has the effect of dropping a dimension and returning a vector.  You could then do the same in the next line.

 

You do also need a returnType statement.

 

The requirement to always explicitly index non-scalar objects is only for model code.  nimbleFunctions do not need that.

 

I also noticed you need to access seas2sim[1] to use it as a scalar.

 

Here is a modification that works:

 

getPopVec <- nimbleFunction(run = function(S = double(1),R = double(1),G = double(2),D = double(2), popVec = double(1),seas2sim = double(1)){
    returnType(double(1))
    pVec <- (G %*% (S*popVec))[,1]
    if(seas2sim[1] == 2) pVec <- (G %*% (S*pVec))[,1] + (D %*% (R*pVec))[,1]
    return(pVec)
})

CgetPopVec <- compileNimble(getPopVec)

 

Does that look like what you need?

Perry

Hi Ben,

 

I was just looking at your previous message to reply and in popped your newest message just now.

 

For a nimbleFunction calling a nimbleFunction, there is a way to return a list and it is called (hah, surprise) a nimbleList.  I think it is relatively little used among nimbleFunction programmers, but it does exist and is important internally and is documented in the User Manual, so let me point you there to start.

 

However, a node in a nimbleModel can't be a nimbleList.  It can only be a (non-scalar) numeric object.  So if you want to use your functions in a model, you would indeed need to break the pieces into different functions.  I think it would look like:

 

nimbleCode({

...

S[1:N] <- Surv_fun_nimbleRcall_version(zr.values[1:A] , zs.values[1:B])

...

})

 

where I don't know the sizes or shapes of your model variables.

 

If there is redundant calculation in the steps needed, you could perhaps use memoize and/or caching methods to check inputs and make use of already calculated results from others of your functions.

 

If you know all of your four pieces (S, R, G, D) only ever need to be calculated at the same time (i.e. they are in the same position in the model graph), some options are (1) you could stack them into one model variable and use indexing to make use of the pieces you need elsewhere, or (2) you could create dummy declarations for all but one of them ( to ensure they exist in the model ) and then make the single non-dummy one have its R function put new values into the others.  That is short-circuiting things but would work fine.  Let me know if that is too cryptic of an explanation.

 

I am not clear what bigmatrix.params is.  I think it is something you'd be accessing not from the model but rather from the R environment, right?

Hi Ben,

 

I don't think I have fully absorbed what you are trying to do, but I'm going to give a hasty answer in case it gives you enough.

 

First, a nimbleRcall really just creates a special wrapper or interface function between nimble and an R function.  That special function is a nimbleFunction, but you don't need to care about that.  The nimbleRcall mechanism is quite general except that inputs and outputs have to be numeric objects.

 

What I'm thinking might be helpful is to realize that you are free from within the nimbleRcall to manipulate the compiled model, or even the compiled samplers, as you wish.  The scheme in very quick outline would be like this:

 

myRfun <- function(x) { # From the nimbleRcall below, nimble will pack up the arguments for this function and take the return value. Otherwise it just calls your R function.

  # within this function, go ahead and manipulate cm if you want. e.g.

  cm$z <- x+1 # now this function sticks a wrench in the model by changing the values of x.  better know what you're doing statistically, but the code should work.

  # etc.

}

 

my_nimbleRcall <- nimbleRcall (myRfun.... etc)

 

m <- nimbleModel(...)

cm <- compileNimble(m). # This is what is used within myRfun

 

If you want to reach inside a sampler and, say, change a member variable, I could show you how to do that too.  But an alternative would be to put a nimbleRcall in the sampler and have it potentially get whatever information it needs from the R environment that way.

 

Again, I'm not quite sure of the complexity you need to solve.  Multiple functions calling multiple scripts doesn't sound like a problem.  You referred to setting starting values -- for what?

 

HTH.  If not, can you maybe say more about the code mechanics you want (regardless of the modeling intent)?

 

Perry

Hi Ben,

 

We try to have errors trapped in R before they result in a C++ compilation failure, but clearly that wasn't successful here.

 

I think it is telling you that "2" is not a vector.  You could change the type declaration for that argument to double(0) or integer(0) (and then use it simply as a vector), or you could put c(2) to turn it into a vector of length 1.  Confusion between true scalars (which don't really exist in R) and length-1 vectors is a point of friction.

 

A good way to test and debug outside of a model is to write a second nimbleFunction to call getPopVec and try compiling them together.  Then you can confirm that how you call it works.  Another debugging route is to make the behavior incomplete and build up bits at a time.  E.g. start with a function that takes one argument and does something trivial and build up from there.  But I'm not saying that we're happy with seeing this slip through error-trapping and give you a C++ error.  It's something we should catch better.

 

HTH

Perry

Hi Ben,

 

Here's my process.  

 

CgetPopVec <- compileNimble(getPopVec)

 

Output is:

Compiling
  [Note] This may take a minute.
  [Note] Use 'showCompilerOutput = TRUE' to see C++ compilation details.
Error: Error, wrong number of indices provided for pVec[1:2500].
 This occurred for: pVec[1:2500]
 This was part of the call:  eigenBlock(ARG1_S_,1:2500) * pVec[1:2500]

 

This error catch tells me pVec has the wrong number of dimensions.

I see pVec is created from

pVec <- G[1:2500,1:2500] %*% (S[1:2500]*popVec)

which will return a matrix.  (This is true in R as well, but R can dynamically treat that later as a vector whereas nimbleFunctions must have statically [unchanging] types.)

There is a section in the user manual on dimension mismatches that can trip people up and how to handle them.  In your case, one solution would be:

 

pVec <- G[1:2500,1:2500] %*% (S[1:2500]*popVec)[,1]

 

where the "[,1]" has the effect of dropping a dimension and returning a vector.  You could then do the same in the next line.

 

You do also need a returnType statement.

 

The requirement to always explicitly index non-scalar objects is only for model code.  nimbleFunctions do not need that.

 

I also noticed you need to access seas2sim[1] to use it as a scalar.

 

Here is a modification that works:

 

getPopVec <- nimbleFunction(run = function(S = double(1),R = double(1),G = double(2),D = double(2), popVec = double(1),seas2sim = double(1)){
    returnType(double(1))
    pVec <- (G %*% (S*popVec))[,1]
    if(seas2sim[1] == 2) pVec <- (G %*% (S*pVec))[,1] + (D %*% (R*pVec))[,1]
    return(pVec)
})

CgetPopVec <- compileNimble(getPopVec)

 

Does that look like what you need?

Perry

Hi Ben,

 

I was just looking at your previous message to reply and in popped your newest message just now.

 

For a nimbleFunction calling a nimbleFunction, there is a way to return a list and it is called (hah, surprise) a nimbleList.  I think it is relatively little used among nimbleFunction programmers, but it does exist and is important internally and is documented in the User Manual, so let me point you there to start.

 

However, a node in a nimbleModel can't be a nimbleList.  It can only be a (non-scalar) numeric object.  So if you want to use your functions in a model, you would indeed need to break the pieces into different functions.  I think it would look like:

 

nimbleCode({

...

S[1:N] <- Surv_fun_nimbleRcall_version(zr.values[1:A] , zs.values[1:B])

...

})

 

where I don't know the sizes or shapes of your model variables.

 

If there is redundant calculation in the steps needed, you could perhaps use memoize and/or caching methods to check inputs and make use of already calculated results from others of your functions.

 

If you know all of your four pieces (S, R, G, D) only ever need to be calculated at the same time (i.e. they are in the same position in the model graph), some options are (1) you could stack them into one model variable and use indexing to make use of the pieces you need elsewhere, or (2) you could create dummy declarations for all but one of them ( to ensure they exist in the model ) and then make the single non-dummy one have its R function put new values into the others.  That is short-circuiting things but would work fine.  Let me know if that is too cryptic of an explanation.

 

I am not clear what bigmatrix.params is.  I think it is something you'd be accessing not from the model but rather from the R environment, right?

 

Perry

First, a nimbleRcall really just creates a special wrapper or interface function between nimble and an R function.  That special function is a nimbleFunction, but you don't need to care about that.  The nimbleRcall mechanism is quite general except that inputs and outputs have to be numeric objects.

 

What I'm thinking might be helpful is to realize that you are free from within the nimbleRcall to manipulate the compiled model, or even the compiled samplers, as you wish.  The scheme in very quick outline would be like this:

 

myRfun <- function(x) { # From the nimbleRcall below, nimble will pack up the arguments for this function and take the return value. Otherwise it just calls your R function.

  # within this function, go ahead and manipulate cm if you want. e.g.

  cm$z <- x+1 # now this function sticks a wrench in the model by changing the values of x.  better know what you're doing statistically, but the code should work.

  # etc.

}

 

my_nimbleRcall <- nimbleRcall (myRfun.... etc)

 

m <- nimbleModel(...)

cm <- compileNimble(m). # This is what is used within myRfun

 

If you want to reach inside a sampler and, say, change a member variable, I could show you how to do that too.  But an alternative would be to put a nimbleRcall in the sampler and have it potentially get whatever information it needs from the R environment that way.

 

Again, I'm not quite sure of the complexity you need to solve.  Multiple functions calling multiple scripts doesn't sound like a problem.  You referred to setting starting values -- for what?

 

HTH.  If not, can you maybe say more about the code mechanics you want (regardless of the modeling intent)?

 

Perry

 

 

On Mon, Aug 22, 2022 at 11:44 AM Ben Padilla <benjamin...@gmail.com> wrote:

Hello All, 

 

I have a somewhat tricky project I am working on that links an integrated population model and integral projection model (ala Plard et al 2019). First, some background and then the tricky integration I could use some guidance on. 

 

Model 1 (IPMpop) is a Bayesian state-space integrated population model. The population I am working on has some demographic data such as estimated population counts, sex ratios, and survival. This model is coded in nimble and uses observed data from the population over the last 25-30 years. 

 

Model 2 (IPMind) is a bio-energetic integral projection model that links individual trait (body  mass and reserve mass) to demographic traits and population size. I am most interested in evaluating the impact of parasites and disease on demographics as mediated by their impact on body condition, so this IPMind is vital. This model is composed of survival, reproduction, growth, and development functions that estimate demographics based on the distribution of body size within the population. The problem is I dont have data for individual body size over time, so this model is based on a simulated initial population, I developed this based on the code of Lachish et al 2020. In its current form, there are a few scripts that are called from a final "run simulations" script to generate model output. 

 

Model 3 is what I am trying to figure out. Essentially, I want to improve the estimates of population size (n females) produced by the IPMind by modeling them as a function of the data in the Bayesian IPMpop. In theory, I could incorporate the IPMind into the Bayesian population model such that the projection kernel estimates population at each time step. For example, in the code below, M is the projection kernel that is estimated by the four R functions packaged into a single 'bigmatrix' function, zr and zs values are the trait value distributions (ie mesh points in an IPMind) and params are the IPM function parameters. So, population size at time t+1 would be a function of growth, survival and reproduction in time t. 

 

for(i in 1:nYears){

M <-  bigmatrix(zr_values, zs_values, params)

indPopVector[i+1]  <- M$G%*%(M$S*indPopVector[i]) + M$D%*%(M$R*indPopVector[i]) 

}

 

So, if that is built into the Bayesian IPMpop model in nimble, I should be able to model that as a function of the observed data with something like this, where ndat is the observed count data. 

for(i in 1:nndat){
    ndat[i,2] ~ T(dnorm(indPopVector[i], ndat[i,4]),0,550000) # Truncated normal
  }

 

In the simplest sense my question is whether it is possible to call external R functions from within a nimble model, or whether all of these would have to be recoded as nimbleFunctions? I have also been looking at the nimbleExternalcall and nimbleRcall functions, but given the complexity of what I have (multiple functions calling multiple scripts that set starting values etc) I am not sure how I'd make that work. 

 

If you've managed to read through to here, thanks! In my mind this seems like it should work, but as I stare into R and try to work out the mechanics of it all I get a bit overwhelmed. Any advice or thoughts will be much appreciated. I am happy to share some code off list if someone really wants to get into the weeds of it with me. 

 

Thanks, 

Ben

Hi Ben,

 

We try to have errors trapped in R before they result in a C++ compilation failure, but clearly that wasn't successful here.

 

I think it is telling you that "2" is not a vector.  You could change the type declaration for that argument to double(0) or integer(0) (and then use it simply as a vector), or you could put c(2) to turn it into a vector of length 1.  Confusion between true scalars (which don't really exist in R) and length-1 vectors is a point of friction.

 

A good way to test and debug outside of a model is to write a second nimbleFunction to call getPopVec and try compiling them together.  Then you can confirm that how you call it works.  Another debugging route is to make the behavior incomplete and build up bits at a time.  E.g. start with a function that takes one argument and does something trivial and build up from there.  But I'm not saying that we're happy with seeing this slip through error-trapping and give you a C++ error.  It's something we should catch better.

 

HTH

Perry

Hi Ben,

 

Here's my process.  

 

CgetPopVec <- compileNimble(getPopVec)

 

Output is:

Compiling
  [Note] This may take a minute.
  [Note] Use 'showCompilerOutput = TRUE' to see C++ compilation details.
Error: Error, wrong number of indices provided for pVec[1:2500].
 This occurred for: pVec[1:2500]
 This was part of the call:  eigenBlock(ARG1_S_,1:2500) * pVec[1:2500]

 

This error catch tells me pVec has the wrong number of dimensions.

I see pVec is created from

pVec <- G[1:2500,1:2500] %*% (S[1:2500]*popVec)

which will return a matrix.  (This is true in R as well, but R can dynamically treat that later as a vector whereas nimbleFunctions must have statically [unchanging] types.)

There is a section in the user manual on dimension mismatches that can trip people up and how to handle them.  In your case, one solution would be:

 

pVec <- G[1:2500,1:2500] %*% (S[1:2500]*popVec)[,1]

 

where the "[,1]" has the effect of dropping a dimension and returning a vector.  You could then do the same in the next line.

 

You do also need a returnType statement.

 

The requirement to always explicitly index non-scalar objects is only for model code.  nimbleFunctions do not need that.

 

I also noticed you need to access seas2sim[1] to use it as a scalar.

 

Here is a modification that works:

 

getPopVec <- nimbleFunction(run = function(S = double(1),R = double(1),G = double(2),D = double(2), popVec = double(1),seas2sim = double(1)){
    returnType(double(1))
    pVec <- (G %*% (S*popVec))[,1]
    if(seas2sim[1] == 2) pVec <- (G %*% (S*pVec))[,1] + (D %*% (R*pVec))[,1]
    return(pVec)
})

CgetPopVec <- compileNimble(getPopVec)

 

Does that look like what you need?

Perry

Hi Ben,

 

I was just looking at your previous message to reply and in popped your newest message just now.

 

For a nimbleFunction calling a nimbleFunction, there is a way to return a list and it is called (hah, surprise) a nimbleList.  I think it is relatively little used among nimbleFunction programmers, but it does exist and is important internally and is documented in the User Manual, so let me point you there to start.

 

However, a node in a nimbleModel can't be a nimbleList.  It can only be a (non-scalar) numeric object.  So if you want to use your functions in a model, you would indeed need to break the pieces into different functions.  I think it would look like:

 

nimbleCode({

...

S[1:N] <- Surv_fun_nimbleRcall_version(zr.values[1:A] , zs.values[1:B])

...

})

 

where I don't know the sizes or shapes of your model variables.

 

If there is redundant calculation in the steps needed, you could perhaps use memoize and/or caching methods to check inputs and make use of already calculated results from others of your functions.

 

If you know all of your four pieces (S, R, G, D) only ever need to be calculated at the same time (i.e. they are in the same position in the model graph), some options are (1) you could stack them into one model variable and use indexing to make use of the pieces you need elsewhere, or (2) you could create dummy declarations for all but one of them ( to ensure they exist in the model ) and then make the single non-dummy one have its R function put new values into the others.  That is short-circuiting things but would work fine.  Let me know if that is too cryptic of an explanation.

 

I am not clear what bigmatrix.params is.  I think it is something you'd be accessing not from the model but rather from the R environment, right?

 

Perry

Hi Ben,

 

I don't think I have fully absorbed what you are trying to do, but I'm going to give a hasty answer in case it gives you enough.

 

First, a nimbleRcall really just creates a special wrapper or interface function between nimble and an R function.  That special function is a nimbleFunction, but you don't need to care about that.  The nimbleRcall mechanism is quite general except that inputs and outputs have to be numeric objects.

 

What I'm thinking might be helpful is to realize that you are free from within the nimbleRcall to manipulate the compiled model, or even the compiled samplers, as you wish.  The scheme in very quick outline would be like this:

 

myRfun <- function(x) { # From the nimbleRcall below, nimble will pack up the arguments for this function and take the return value. Otherwise it just calls your R function.

  # within this function, go ahead and manipulate cm if you want. e.g.

  cm$z <- x+1 # now this function sticks a wrench in the model by changing the values of x.  better know what you're doing statistically, but the code should work.

  # etc.

}

 

my_nimbleRcall <- nimbleRcall (myRfun.... etc)

 

m <- nimbleModel(...)

cm <- compileNimble(m). # This is what is used within myRfun

 

If you want to reach inside a sampler and, say, change a member variable, I could show you how to do that too.  But an alternative would be to put a nimbleRcall in the sampler and have it potentially get whatever information it needs from the R environment that way.

 

Again, I'm not quite sure of the complexity you need to solve.  Multiple functions calling multiple scripts doesn't sound like a problem.  You referred to setting starting values -- for what?

 

HTH.  If not, can you maybe say more about the code mechanics you want (regardless of the modeling intent)?

 

Perry
